topics.title: Chapter 55 — Program Optimization
topics.summary: Optimization changes an implementation while preserving its required behavior. The largest improvements often come from doing less work, moving fewer bytes, or avoiding repeated setup. Low-level instruction tuning is valuable only when the relevant instructions materially contribute to the measured bottleneck. Use a sequence of verified changes. Keep the original implementation as a reference when possible, compare outputs on normal and boundary cases, and measure each candidate under the same workload. A performance improvement that changes the result has not met the same specification. [ R2 ]

topics.title: 55.1 Algorithmic optimization
topics.summary: Algorithmic optimization changes the amount or organization of required work. Replacing repeated scans with an index, using a better asymptotic algorithm, or precomputing reusable summaries can dominate instruction-level changes. Account for construction and update costs. An index that makes queries fast may be inappropriate when the dataset changes constantly and only one query is performed. Optimize the complete workload, including the frequency of preprocessing and maintenance.

topics.title: 55.2 Compiler optimization
topics.summary: Compiler options enable transformations such as inlining, vectorization, and dead-code elimination. The compiler relies on language rules, available definitions, aliasing information, and target architecture. More aggressive flags can change assumptions or numerical behavior. Distinguish ordinary optimization levels from options that relax floating-point semantics or target instructions unavailable on another machine. Record the exact build configuration with results instead of describing it only as a “release build.”

topics.title: 55.3 Memory optimization
topics.summary: Memory optimization reduces allocation overhead, footprint, copying, and unnecessary lifetime extension. Reusing buffers can help when ownership is clear and retained capacity remains bounded. Do not trade a modest allocation reduction for dangling references or uncontrolled memory retention. A cache of reusable objects needs an eviction and size policy. Peak memory includes temporarily duplicated data during transformations, not merely the final representation.

topics.title: 55.4 Cache optimization
topics.summary: Cache optimization improves useful reuse and reduces transferred irrelevant bytes. Blocking, compact indexes, and traversal changes can help. The working set includes all simultaneously active data, not just the main input array. Measure the effect on total runtime and verify that a cache-focused change does not increase computation or synchronization enough to offset its benefit. Counter changes are evidence about mechanisms, not a replacement for the application’s completion metric.

topics.title: 55.5 Reducing allocations
topics.summary: Repeated small allocations can add allocator work, fragmentation, and cache misses. Reserving known capacity, using stack storage for bounded small objects, or allocating from a scoped arena can reduce those costs. Each technique changes lifetime or memory-use tradeoffs. Reserving too much wastes capacity; stack storage has size limits; arenas often reclaim everything together. Choose a mechanism whose ownership model matches the data’s actual lifetime.

topics.title: 55.6 Batching
topics.summary: Batching amortizes setup, synchronization, and I/O overhead across several items. A batch can also expose vectorization or parallel work. It is especially useful when one operation has a large fixed cost relative to each item’s incremental cost. Batch size is a tuning parameter constrained by latency and memory. A service that waits indefinitely to fill a batch can harm low-volume clients. Use a maximum size and a maximum waiting policy when responsiveness matters.

topics.title: Worked example — Prefix sums replace repeated scans
topics.summary: Suppose a fixed array must answer many sum queries over half-open ranges [begin, end) . A direct scan costs work proportional to each range length. A prefix array stores prefix[k] = sum of elements before k , allowing a query to return prefix[end] - prefix[begin] after validation. For nonnegative bounded values whose total fits uint64_t , prefix construction is linear and each query is constant-time. Signed or floating-point data require additional numeric analysis: overflow and subtraction behavior must match the intended specification. Companion listing: ch55/range_sums.cpp The three query results are 45, 45, and 4500, for a combined 4590. The optimization changes repeated work from scanning every queried element to one preprocessing pass plus constant work per query. It uses extra memory and becomes less attractive when updates invalidate the prefix array frequently.
